oil.summary: Crude held narrow gains on the day — WTI +0.24% to $79.84, Brent +0.14% to $85.07 — but the week-on-week surge of roughly 11% tells the real story. The Strait of Hormuz is under full-conflict conditions: Iranian missiles struck Emirati tankers, three vessels were damaged in the Gulf, and U.S. forces this morning disabled an Iran-linked tanker near Kharg Island. Despite that escalatory ladder, spot crude is exhibiting notable fatigue at current levels, with Brent described as slipping even as strikes continue. The divergence is sharp in products: RBOB collapsed 5.97% on the session while Heating Oil shed 1.30%, though HO's one-month gain of 19.3% reflects the Ukraine-driven dismantling of Russian refining capacity. Secondary pressure points include U.S. secondary tariffs on Indian and Chinese buyers of Russian crude — eased from 500% to 100% — and TotalEnergies flagging stronger Q2 refining margins.
drivers: Hormuz risk premium: multiple tanker strikes and U.S. military action near Kharg Island keep geopolitical floor elevated, yet crude showing diminishing upside sensitivity to each new escalation
Ukrainian strikes on Russian refining infrastructure have pushed Moscow's crude processing to a 21-year low, tightening global middle-distillate supply and underpinning Heating Oil's 19% monthly gain
U.S. secondary tariff policy on Russian oil buyers in flux — rate cut from 500% to 100% for India and China — introducing trade-flow uncertainty at the margin

gas.summary: The Henry Hub/TTF divergence is stark today. Henry Hub fell 1.74% to $2.871/MMBtu and is down 8.71% on the month, reflecting ample domestic U.S. supply conditions. TTF moved in the opposite direction, gaining 2.63% to €54.353/MWh and posting a 10.87% weekly advance and 16.21% monthly surge — entirely consistent with the Hormuz supply shock bleeding into LNG markets. Asian spot LNG prices jumped 10% in the past week to their highest since March, and Pakistan's state buyer paid the highest spot LNG price in four years as Qatari supply falters amid the Middle East escalation. The feed-gas disruption risk from the Hormuz corridor is the dominant driver; Henry Hub's weakness shows the crisis has not yet redirected enough U.S. LNG export demand to tighten the domestic balance.
drivers: Hormuz crisis is disrupting Qatari LNG flows, driving Asian spot LNG up 10% on the week to the highest level since March
Pakistan paid the highest spot LNG price in four years, illustrating acute procurement stress for price-sensitive emerging market buyers
Henry Hub continues to weaken (-8.71% month-on-month), as U.S. domestic supply remains well-supplied and the global price spike has not yet materially tightened the Henry Hub balance

power.summary: The power and carbon complex offers a mixed picture with thin sector-specific price flow. EU EUAs slipped 2.57% to $74.84, broadly flat on the week and month, suggesting the carbon market is not yet pricing a sustained gas-to-coal switching premium despite TTF's 16% monthly rise. On the structural demand side, U.S. electricity consumption hit a new record in 2025 and is tracking for further all-time highs this year and next, driven by AI data-center load growth — a trend also spurring a 69% surge in global nuclear fusion investment to a record $4.48 billion in 2025. China connected the world's largest hybrid solar plant to the grid. India hiked diesel and jet fuel export taxes for the July 16 fortnight, citing the Hormuz crisis tightening refined product availability. Tehran's warnings of strikes on regional energy infrastructure add tail risk across the sector.
drivers: AI-driven U.S. power demand hit record highs in 2025 and is set for further gains, structurally tightening the grid and accelerating long-duration energy investment including a record $4.48B in fusion funding
EU EUAs down 2.57% on the day despite TTF surging 16% over the month, suggesting carbon markets are not yet fully pricing gas-to-coal switching or a sustained supply disruption premium

Geopolitical tail risk remains elevated: Tehran has threatened strikes on regional energy infrastructure, and India's export duty hike on diesel and jet fuel signals tightening of refined product flows tied to the Hormuz crisis
